messages.content: Can you arrange a flight for me from New York, NY to Paris with a departure on the 20th of June 2022 at 5 in the afternoon?

function.name: book_flight
function.description: Books a flight based on the provided departure location and time. Optionally, a return time can be specified for round-trip bookings. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

departure_location.description: The departure location in the format of 'City (abbr), State', such as 'Los Angeles, CA' or 'New York, NY'.

departure_time.description: The departure time in the format of 'dd/mm/yyyy HH:MM', representing the local time of the departure location.

return_time.description: The return time in the format of 'dd/mm/yyyy HH:MM', representing the local time of the departure location. If not specified, a one-way ticket is booked.

message.reasoning:
The user wants to arrange a flight from New York, NY to Paris with departure on 20th June 2022 at 5 PM. We need to use the function "book_flight". Provide departure_location: "New York, NY" presumably. But we also need arrival location? The function signature only includes departure_location, departure_time, optional return_time. It doesn't include destination. So maybe it's assumed that booking is from departure_location to some predetermined destination? That seems odd.

But given the tool's definition, it expects just those parameters; perhaps the system knows the destination implicitly? Or maybe there's an error. However, we should call the function with the available arguments. There's no mention of specifying destination. We'll proceed accordingly.

We will provide departure_location="New York, NY", departure_time="20/06/2022 17:00".

Return_time unspecified -> None.

We'll then invoke the function.
